ATTORNEY GENERAL TONG URGES CONNECTICUT INSURANCE DEPARTMENT TO REJECT DOUBLE-DIGIT HEALTH INSURANCE RATE HIKE REQUESTS
(Hartford, CT) – In a letter today to Connecticut Insurance Commissioner Josh Hershman, Attorney General William Tong urged the rejection of double-digit rate hikes sought by Anthem, ConnectiCare and UnitedHealthcare for individual and small group plans covering approximately 220,000 people across Connecticut.
The Connecticut Insurance Department will hold a public information session on the rate requests beginning at 9 a.m. on Wednesday August 26 at the Legislative Office Building.
“These insurers are, once again, requesting rate increases that exceed other inflationary and general economic growth measures. To put it bluntly: never-ending insurance rate increases reflect a broken system that does not deliver affordable healthcare for the struggling citizens of Connecticut. Once again, these increases and plan design changes project another year of consumers getting less for more,” Attorney General Tong states in his letter.
Attorney General Tong’s letter commends the Insurance Department for assessing not just the actuarial underpinning of the rates, but also the underlying cost drivers of those rates, including ever-rising prescription drug costs, reimbursements to large health systems that are increasingly consolidated and corporatized.
Attorney General Tong takes the insurance carriers to task for failing to ensure their reimbursement rates reflect actual costs of service, and for failing to show they are curbing upcoding and fraudulent billing practices – by returning those savings to consumers.
“Consumers are paying significant out of pocket costs and –believe me – they notice when they have to pay a substantial deductible charge for a service they did not ask for and did not receive. It is not uncommon for my Office to hear from patients when they notice they were charged for an emergency department visit after receiving care at an urgent care center or billed at an acuity level reflecting a life-threatening condition that did not match their non-life threatening symptoms,” Attorney General Tong states.
Attorney General Tong’s letter calls out ConnectiCare for the mismanagement of the migration of its claims payment systems to Molina Healthcare. “It is deeply concerning that the carrier requesting the highest increases should have provided some of the worst customer service during that transition and should have been so ill prepared for that transition many months after its acquisition was approved by the Connecticut Insurance Department,” Attorney General Tong states.
For individual plans, Anthem is seeking an average increase of 12.8 percent. ConnectiCare is seeking an average increase of 22.7 for individual plans. For small group plans, Anthem is seeking an average increase of 17.4. United Healthcare is seeking an average increase of 18.9 percent.
Pursuant to Connecticut law, in order for these rates to be approved, the Connecticut Insurance Department must determine that these requested rates are not “excessive, inadequate, or unfairly discriminatory.”
Assistant Attorney General Tom Ryan assisted the Attorney General in this matter.

More US employers to drop weight-loss drugs in 2027, as healthcare costs increase
About 14% of employers in the United States have already or plan to drop GLP-1 drugs in 2027, as companies see rising healthcare costs, according to a survey released on Tuesday by the Business Group on ​Health. Healthcare costs are set to increase 9.2% if employers do not make changes to manage costs in 2027, up from 8.5% in 2026, the group said. Two-thirds of employers surveyed said they saw rising utilization of the drugs.
BioNTech ​halts mRNA colorectal cancer vaccine trial after safety review
BioNTech SE said it will end a mid-stage study of its experimental mRNA cancer vaccine after an ‌independent committee found the ​treatment was unlikely to help colorectal cancer patients live longer, sending the company's U.S.-listed shares 7.5% lower on Friday. The trial was testing whether the immunotherapy, autogene cevumeran, prevented a recurrence in patients with high-risk, mid-stage colorectal cancer who had already undergone surgery but still had traces of cancer DNA in their blood.
US FDA approves Lilly's Mounjaro to reduce cardiovascular risk
Eli Lilly said on Friday the U.S. FDA has approved its diabetes drug Mounjaro to reduce the chances of heart attack or stroke in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk of cardiovascular events. The approval expands the use of Mounjaro, which targets the GLP-1 protein, beyond blood sugar control. In the U.S., Lilly sells the obesity version of the drug under the brand Zepbound.
Analysis-Moderna, Merck ‌breakthrough could usher in wave of cancer vaccines
Merck and Moderna's success with a personalized cancer vaccine designed to keep melanoma at bay opens a new avenue of treatment that doctors hope will work against many types of tumors. Unlike chemotherapy, which kills both healthy and cancerous cells, or immunotherapy, which revs up the immune system, personalized cancer vaccines train the immune system to specifically target mutations found only on a person's tumor.
Meta settlement falls short on teen mental health protections, whistleblower says
A whistleblower whose testimony helped build a child safety case against Meta Platforms said on Wednesday that the firm's settlement with a coalition of U.S. states does not meaningfully address harms from social media that he described in court. Former Meta safety engineer Arturo Bejar told a judge and eight jurors last week that the firm had knowingly underreported the frequency with which teens were harmed on its platforms, pushed them toward content that made them feel bad about themselves and failed to correctly adjudicate reports of child predation.
US FDA approves Roivant-Priovant's skin and muscle disease drug
The U.S. ‌Food and Drug Administration said on Thursday it approved a treatment from Roivant and partner Priovant Therapeutics for a rare disease, making it the first oral drug for the condition affecting skin and muscles. Shares of Roivant closed up 2% at $37.58 in afternoon trading.
US widens lettuce-related cyclosporiasis probe to 20 states
U.S. health authorities have widened their probe into a cyclosporiasis outbreak tied to iceberg lettuce from central Mexico after detecting cases in three additional states, raising the total to 20 states, ‌the FDA and CDC said on Thursday. The outbreak, linked to iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants and sourced from Taylor Farms' operations in Mexico, has grown to 11,458 cases, including 495 hospitalizations.
US FDA approves Takeda, Protagonist's drug for rare blood cancer
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a first-of-its-kind drug from Takeda Pharmaceutical and Protagonist Therapeutics to treat a rare blood cancer, the health regulator said on Friday. The approval of rusfertide brings a highly anticipated, less-invasive treatment option for thousands of patients who have historically relied on frequent bloodletting procedures to manage their condition.
Explainer-What to know about postpartum mental illness
After a month-long trial, a Massachusetts jury is deciding the fate of Lindsay Clancy, a mother who killed her three young children in 2023 and then tried to kill herself. Her defense lawyer says her actions were due to her suffering from the most severe form of postpartum mental illness, while a prosecutor called the tragedy a planned murder. Here is what to know about the range of mental health conditions that are associated with childbirth:
China approves J&J psoriasis pill Icotyde, says drugmaker
China's drug regulator has approved Johnson & Johnson's oral pill for psoriasis, the company said on Thursday, intensifying competition in the world's second-largest pharmaceutical market with rivals including Bristol Myers ⁠Squibb and AbbVie. Psoriasis, a chronic ​autoimmune condition that causes itchy, scaly, and inflamed patches of skin, affects more than 8.4 million patients in China, according to J&J. Other ⁠treatments include its own Tremfya, Bristol Myers' Sotyktu and AbbVie's Skyrizi.
Measles cases in Pennsylvania rise to 460 amid ongoing outbreak
Pennsylvania's health department said on Friday the confirmed number of cases linked to a measles outbreak has reached 460 this year, an increase of 36 over its update two days ago. Two Pennsylvania residents have died after contracting the highly contagious disease — the first such deaths reported in the United States in 2026 — as cases reach their highest level in more than three decades.
Walmart settles US government's opioid lawsuit, Justice Department says
Walmart has settled a U.S. government lawsuit accusing the retailer of fueling a nationwide opioid ⁠epidemic by unlawfully dispensing prescriptions from its pharmacies, the Department of Justice said on Friday. Terms were not immediately available.
Health Round: Younger lung cancer patients more easily matched to targeted therapies

Kimberly-Clark seeks EU approval for $40 billion Kenvue deal
Kimberly-Clark has asked EU regulators permission for its proposed $40 billion takeover of Tylenol maker Kenvue, documents on the EU Commission's website showed. Kimberly-Clark announced the takeover in November last year.
FDA allows marketing of Juul's new e-cigarettes and ​flavored pods
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Friday authorized the marketing of three new 'JUUL2' e-cigarette products, the latest in a series of approvals for nicotine products the agency says may offer a lower-risk alternative to traditional cigarettes. Here are some details:
Walmart settles US government's opioid lawsuit, which sought billions, for $50 million
Walmart will pay $50 million to settle a U.S. government lawsuit accusing the nation's largest retailer of fueling a nationwide opioid epidemic by unlawfully dispensing prescriptions from its ⁠pharmacies, the Department of Justice said on Friday. The payout is far less than the billions of dollars in civil penalties that the Justice Department had said Walmart could owe when the lawsuit began in December 2020, near the end of President Donald Trump's first White House term.
Biopharma firm BioXcel Therapeutics files for bankruptcy in US
AI-driven biopharma firm BioXcel Therapeutics filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the U.S. on Thursday. Here are more details:
Roivant, Priovant launch newly approved rare disease drug Lisraya at $35,000 a month
Roivant and partner Priovant Therapeutics on Friday set a list price of $35,000 for a 30-day supply of their newly approved rare disease drug, Lisraya. Here are ⁠the details:
LeapFrog ​plans up to $100 million in India healthcare investments over two years
Global private equity firm LeapFrog Investments plans to invest $80 million to $100 million in India's healthcare sector over the next two years, a top executive told Reuters, as it seeks to benefit from the rising demand for medical services. Expanding insurance coverage and greater use of diagnostics and preventive care in a country with high rates of chronic disease have boosted healthcare spending. India's healthcare sector was valued at about $180 billion in 2023 and is expected to grow to $320 billion by 2028, government data showed.
Congo starts Ebola vaccinations for health workers
Democratic Republic of Congo on Thursday began vaccinating frontline health workers with a vaccine approved for a different Ebola species, as authorities seek to contain the country's largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak on record. Health Minister Samuel-Roger Kamba said Congo had received more than 50,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine and would begin vaccinations in provinces affected by the outbreak, prioritising health workers.
Aid group MSF opens new Ebola treatment ⁠centre in eastern Congo
French aid group Medecins Sans Frontieres said on Friday it had opened a new Ebola treatment centre in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Bed shortages are seen as one of many challenges in controlling the outbreak, which is the second deadliest ever and outpacing containment efforts.
Cytokinetics heart drug shows promise in trial, but analysts question modest benefits
Cytokinetics said on Friday detailed late-stage data showed its drug, aficamten, significantly improved symptoms and exercise capacity in patients with a genetic ⁠heart condition that currently has no approved treatments. Its shares, however, fell 6% as Wall Street analysts focused on the treatment's modest benefits and safety concerns.
US ⁠FDA approves Gilead's once-daily combination pill for HIV treatment
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Gilead Sciences' once-daily oral combination pill for treatment of adults whose HIV infection has already been reduced to very low levels, the company said on Thursday. The drug, branded Bixlenvo, combines Gilead's HIV medicines bictegravir and lenacapavir.
Forced birth control in Greenland violated women's rights but didn't constitute genocide, experts find
A campaign of forced contraception in Greenland that ran primarily in the 1960s and 1970s violated women's human rights but did not meet the legal definition of genocide, two expert reports concluded on Friday. Both found administering contraception without valid consent breached the women's right to respect for their private and family life and subjected them to degrading treatment in some cases. The ‌reports differed on whether the practice was systemic.
US FDA approves updated COVID vaccines for 2026-27 ‌season
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna, Novavax-Sanofi and Pfizer-BioNTech's updated COVID vaccines, the companies said on Thursday, after an advisory panel recommended that the shots should target the dominant XFG variant. Four COVID shots had been approved for use in the ​United States: Moderna's mNEXSPIKE and Spikevax, Pfizer-BioNTech's, Comirnaty — all three mRNA-based vaccines — and Novavax-Sanofi's, protein-based shot that takes longer to manufacture.

Pharma Policy.content:
₹2.5 lakh to ₹8,800: The Kurien order that made patent history
PH Kurien’s order on the cancer drug Nexavar was a defining moment in India’s public-health movement. No other medicine has since received a compulsory licence amid continuing pressure from multinational pharmaceutical companies.
Dileep V Kumar
Published Aug 29, 2026 | 4:53 PM
⚊
Updated Aug 29, 2026 | 4:53 PM
Share
PH Kurien, Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks.
Make Us Your Preferred Source on Google
Synopsis:
PH Kurien’s landmark 2012 order granting Natco Pharma a compulsory licence to sell a far cheaper version of Bayer’s cancer drug Nexavar became a defining moment in India’s battle to make life-saving medicines affordable and accessible. Issued on his last day as the country’s top patent official, the decision challenged the limits of patent protection while putting patients’ access to essential cancer treatment at the heart of the debate.
When PH Kurien signed the order allowing a domestic drugmaker to sell a cheaper version of a multinational company’s cancer medicine, he made a decision that would outlive his tenure as India’s top patent official.
Issued on his last day in office in March 2012, the 68-page order granted India’s first compulsory licence for a patented drug and put the affordability of a life-saving medicine at the centre of a landmark patent dispute.
Kurien, who died on 27 August in Thiruvananthapuram at the age of 67, had by then spent more than two decades in the civil service, serving in key positions in Keralam and at the Centre.
His career took him from administration and information technology to revenue and disaster management, including a key role in the state’s response to the 2018 floods.
But the Nexavar ruling gave his name wider resonance, turning an administrative decision into a landmark in India’s public-health and patent history.
The order followed a battle between Natco Pharma and Bayer over sorafenib tosylate, marketed as Nexavar, a drug used to treat advanced kidney and liver cancers. Bayer was charging about ₹2.5 lakh for a month’s treatment, while Natco proposed to sell the same treatment for ₹8,800.
Natco argued that Bayer was not making the drug available to enough patients, its price was beyond the reach of most Indians who needed it, and that the patent was not being adequately worked in India. Kurien’s order accepted all three grounds and allowed Natco to manufacture and market the generic version, subject to conditions including a royalty payment to Bayer.
For Kurien, the decision came at the end of his tenure as Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks. For India, it became a test of how far patent protection should extend when the price and availability of a medicine put it beyond the reach of the people who needed it.
Also Read:
A cancer drug, a patent and Article 21
The battle for access to Nexavar
The dispute that eventually led to India’s landmark compulsory licence for Bayer’s cancer drug Nexavar began in August 2011.
It followed after Indian generic drugmaker Natco Pharma approached the Controller of Patents, seeking a compulsory licence to manufacture and sell sorafenib tosylate, a patented drug used to treat advanced kidney and liver cancers, sold under the brand name Nexavar.
Bayer, which had developed the drug with California-based biotechnology company Onyx Pharmaceuticals, mounted a determined legal challenge to Natco’s bid.
The German pharmaceutical giant first sought a stay of the compulsory licence proceedings before the patent office.
When that effort failed to halt the process, Bayer moved the Bombay and Delhi High Courts, challenging the Controller’s initial finding that the case appeared fit for consideration of a compulsory licence.
The courts eventually allowed Bayer to contest the
prima facie
findings before the patent office itself, setting the stage for a prolonged battle over whether Natco should be allowed to enter the market.
Natco’s case rested on three central grounds: that Bayer had failed to make the drug available in adequate quantities in India, the medicine was priced beyond the reach of most patients, and the patented invention was not being worked in India.
After a series of hearings marked by strong objections from Bayer, the Patent Office accepted all three grounds and granted Natco the compulsory licence.
Nexavar belongs to a class of compounds known as carboxyaryl-substituted diphenyl ureas and was developed for patients suffering from renal cell carcinoma, a form of kidney cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma, the most common primary cancer of the liver.
The drug is not generally described as a cure. It is used mainly to slow the progression of advanced cancers and ease the burden of the disease. Clinical studies showed that the drug could extend survival by a median of roughly three months in certain patients with advanced kidney or liver cancer.
For Bayer, the case was about protecting the value of years of research and development and the patent rights attached to the drug. For Natco, it became a test of whether those patent rights could take precedence when a life-saving medicine remained unaffordable and insufficiently available to patients in India.
That clash between patent protection and access to essential medicines would make the Nexavar case one of the most closely watched compulsory-licensing battles in India.
Also Read:
Generic Semaglutide launches in India after patent expiry
₹2.5 lakh vs ₹8,800: Natco challenges Bayer’s Nexavar pricing
Natco Pharma challenged Bayer Corporation’s patent over the cancer drug Nexavar, arguing that the German company had failed to make the medicine adequately available and affordable to Indian patients.
Natco pointed out that Bayer was supplying the drug to only about 2% of the nearly 88,000 patients estimated to need it.
This, it argued, fell far short of the requirement under India’s Patents Act that a patented medicine should meet the “reasonable requirements of the public”.
The company also questioned Bayer’s pricing of Nexavar.
A month’s treatment was being sold for around ₹2.8 lakh, while Natco said it could supply the same quantity for ₹8,800.
At the time Natco filed its application, Bayer’s price was about ₹2,50,428 for a month’s treatment.
Natco further contended that Bayer was not producing the drug in sufficient quantities in India and, therefore, had not met the statutory “working” requirement under the Patents Act.
Availability was another concern. Natco said Nexavar was accessible only in a limited number of States, mainly through major metropolitan centres, leaving patients in places such as Madhya Pradesh and several parts of Maharashtra without adequate access.
Before seeking a compulsory licence, Natco said it had approached Bayer for a voluntary licence to manufacture and market the drug in India. Bayer rejected the request, leaving Natco to move the authorities for a compulsory licence under Section 84(1) of the Patents Act, 1970, read with Rule 96 of the Patent Rules, 2003.
Also Read:
Johnson & Johnson bid to extend TB drug Bedaquiline patent rejected
A landmark patent ruling
The decision came on 9 March 2012 — the final day in office for Kurian as Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks.
It proved to be a consequential closing chapter to his tenure, as the Indian Patent Office granted Natco Pharma the country’s first compulsory licence to manufacture and market an anti-cancer drug.
After examining the evidence and hearing arguments from both sides, Kurian delivered what was widely regarded as a landmark, carefully reasoned order in favour of Natco. The ruling, which runs into 68 pages, opened the door for a domestic manufacturer to produce Bayer’s patented cancer drug Nexavar at a substantially lower price.
A key question before the Patent Office was whether Bayer was meeting the “reasonable requirements of the public”, as required under India’s Patents Act. The authority found that it was not. According to the evidence placed before it, Bayer’s supply of Nexavar was reaching only about two per cent of the patients who needed the drug.
The Patent Office relied heavily on Bayer’s statements of working for the three calendar years following the grant of the patent. Those records indicated that the quantity of Nexavar imported into India was far below what was required to meet the needs of the country’s patients.
Bayer argued that sales of the drug by Cipla, which it accused of infringement, should also be considered while assessing whether the public’s requirements were being met. The Patent Office rejected that argument.
Price was another decisive factor.
Bayer was selling a month’s supply of Nexavar for about ₹2.8 lakh, a price the Patent Office considered beyond the reach of ordinary patients. It concluded that the public was not purchasing the drug because its price was not affordable.
Bayer maintained that pharmaceutical research and development involved enormous expenditure and that continued investment was necessary to develop new medicines. It also argued that affordability could not be judged uniformly, given the different economic circumstances of various sections of society.
The Patent Office acknowledged these arguments but found that they did not outweigh the evidence on affordability.
The ruling also settled an important question over what constitutes “working” of a patent in India.
The Patent Office held that merely importing a patented product into the country could not, by itself, amount to working the patent as contemplated under the Patents Act, 1970.
In reaching that conclusion, the authority examined the relevant provisions of Indian patent law alongside the Paris Convention and the TRIPS Agreement. It interpreted the requirement that a patent be “worked in the territory of India” as requiring manufacture in India to a reasonable extent, rather than simply bringing the patented product into the country.
The decision thus went beyond the immediate dispute between Bayer and Natco. It underscored the balance Indian patent law seeks to strike between exclusive patent rights and the wider public interest — particularly when the availability and affordability of essential medicines are at stake.
‘A defining moment for public health’: Ekbal recalls PH Kurien
Public health activist Dr B Ekbal remembered Kurien’s role in the compulsory licensing case.
Dr Ekbal noted that Kurien’s decision drew not only on the submissions of the two companies but also on views and material from international health organisations, including the World Health Organisation and UNICEF, and experts such as Carlos Correa and James Love.
He said the order went beyond the immediate patent dispute, documenting what he described as the aggressive pricing practices and marketing strategies of multinational drug companies. It also recorded the profits Bayer earned from the sale of the cancer medicine and highlighted the difficulty patients faced in accessing it.
Bayer challenged the decision before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The board, headed by Justice Prabha Sreedevan, rejected the challenge on 3 February 2013, holding that compulsory licensing was justified to ensure the drug was available to the public at a reasonable price.
Dr Ekbal described Kurien’s order as a defining moment in India’s public-health movement and noted that no other medicine has since received a compulsory licence amid continuing pressure from multinational pharmaceutical companies.

Pharma Policy.url_match_title: Mounjaro Approved for Heart Attack, Stroke Risk in Diabetes Patients - 조선일보
Pharma Policy.content:
Eli Lilly’s diabetes treatment ‘Mounjaro’ has expanded its usage in the U.S. as a therapy to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular diseases, including myocardial infarction and stroke. As GLP-1 class treatments, which have rapidly grown as obesity and diabetes therapies, broaden their scope to cardiovascular and kidney diseases, global pharmaceutical companies are intensifying competition to preempt the market.
Eli Lilly announced on August 28 (local time) that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted additional approval for Mounjaro to lower the risk of cardiovascular death and non-fatal myocardial infarction or stroke in adults with type 2 diabetes at high risk of cardiovascular disease.
The active ingredient in Mounjaro, tirzepatide, is a dual-acting drug that simultaneously utilizes the effects of GIP and GLP-1, two hormones involved in reducing appetite and lowering blood sugar. In the U.S., it is sold as ‘Mounjaro’ for diabetes treatment and ‘Zepbound’ for obesity treatment.
The approval was based on a large-scale clinical trial by Eli Lilly involving 13,299 patients with diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Patients were tracked for approximately four years across 640 medical institutions in 30 countries. Unlike a placebo, Mounjaro was directly compared with Eli Lilly’s existing treatment ‘Trulicity,’ which has proven cardiovascular protective effects. The incidence rate of major cardiovascular diseases was 12.2% in the Mounjaro group, lower than the 13.1% in the Trulicity group. Calculations reflecting individual follow-up periods and disease onset times showed an 8% lower risk of disease occurrence in the Mounjaro group compared to the existing treatment. However, it was not proven to be more effective.
Danish pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, known for ‘Wegovy,’ is also focusing on expanding its treatments to cardiovascular and kidney diseases. In 2024, Novo Nordisk received FDA approval for Wegovy to reduce cardiovascular death and myocardial infarction or stroke risks in overweight or obese adults with cardiovascular disease. Last year, its oral diabetes treatment ‘Rybelsus’ was also approved to lower major cardiovascular disease risks in diabetic patients at high cardiovascular risk.
This expansion of indications directly impacts insurance and prescription competition in the GLP-1 treatment market. Insurers are reducing coverage for GLP-1 obesity treatments aimed at weight loss due to high costs. Conversely, recognition of non-weight-loss therapeutic effects, such as for cardiovascular diseases, makes it easier to expand insurance coverage. Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk are also conducting clinical trials to broaden treatment areas to obesity-related conditions like fatty liver, sleep apnea, and heart failure.

Hair Loss Treatments Are Wall Street's New Gold Mine? Related Stocks Surge 500%
Add to Google Preferred Sources
The hair loss treatment market, which has seen no new drug approvals in decades, has emerged as a fresh focus for Wall Street. An estimated 50 million men and 30 million women in the U.S. suffer from hereditary hair loss, yet the last FDA approval for a new treatment came in the late 1990s. In this void, Veradermics has seen its stock surge roughly 500% since its February IPO, while Absci has more than doubled this year. Cosmo plans to file for FDA approval of its topical hair loss treatment clascoterone in the first quarter of 2027, with Jefferies projecting global sales could reach $3 billion. Analysts point to side effect concerns with existing treatments and the high cost of hair transplants as key demand drivers for new therapies. However, unlike obesity drugs, hair loss treatments are unlikely to secure insurance coverage, meaning consumers would likely bear the full cost. The inherent risk of clinical failure in drug development also remains a significant caveat.

The success story of GLP-1 drugs that ignited the obesity treatment boom is now fueling expectations that a similar phenomenon could unfold in the hair loss treatment market. With clinical results being announced in rapid succession in a field that has seen no new treatment options for decades, stocks of related biotech companies are soaring.
An estimated 50 million men and 30 million women in the United States suffer from hereditary hair loss. Yet the last time the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a new hair loss treatment was in the late 1990s. In effect, no new drug has reached the market in nearly 30 years.
New drug candidates emerging in this void are capturing investor attention. U.S.-based hair loss drug developer Veradermics has seen its stock climb approximately 500% since its initial public offering (IPO) in February. AI-driven drug discovery company Absci has also more than doubled its share price this year.
Swiss pharmaceutical company Cosmo has drawn attention after reporting positive results in clinical trials for its male pattern baldness treatment. The topical hair loss drug 'clascoterone,' which Cosmo is developing, works by directly blocking the action of hormones that cause male pattern baldness at the hair follicle. The treatment uses the same active ingredient as Winlevi, which Cosmo currently sells as an acne treatment.
Cosmo has described clascoterone as potentially its "single largest opportunity" among its product portfolio and plans to file for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027. Global investment bank Jefferies projects that Cosmo's male hair loss treatment could generate $3 billion (approximately 4.1 trillion won) in worldwide sales. Analysts see room for Cosmo's stock to nearly double from current levels over the next 12 months.
Limitations of Existing Treatments and the Market Opportunity
Wall Street's focus on the hair loss market stems from the clear limitations of existing treatments. The primary medications currently used by hair loss patients are topical minoxidil and oral Propecia (finasteride). However, minoxidil carries concerns about heart palpitations, while finasteride has been linked to decreased libido. Hair transplants are expensive and carry significant surgical burden.
Needham analyst Gil Blum noted, "People fly to Turkey to get hair transplants. What if you could get the same effect without a transplant?" Wall Street's view is that if a treatment with fewer side effects and greater convenience emerges, consumers are likely to pay out of pocket even without insurance coverage.
This mirrors the explosive growth trajectory of the GLP-1 obesity drug market. The success of GLP-1 drugs pushed Eli Lilly's market capitalization past $1 trillion (approximately 1,371.5 trillion won), and Novo Nordisk at one point became Europe's most valuable company. Pharmaceutical companies and investors are betting that a similar blockbuster opportunity could emerge in the hair loss treatment market.
Veradermics announced positive results in April from clinical trials of an oral minoxidil formulation for male pattern baldness, and in July confirmed potential in trials involving female hair loss patients. If approved by the FDA, it could become the first oral medication approved for female pattern hair loss. Absci is developing 'ABS-201,' an injectable hair loss treatment designed by AI, and plans to release interim clinical results in the second half of this year.
Potential for Multiple Winners to Coexist
There are expectations that the hair loss market may accommodate multiple treatments rather than being dominated by a single company. Jefferies analyst Roger Song said, "Hair loss patients tend to use multiple prescription and over-the-counter products together if they can afford it. This market can accommodate multiple treatments."
Jeff Su, portfolio manager at Orbimed, commented, "Obesity and hair loss are both large consumer markets, and that's one reason both areas offer substantial revenue potential. If you find a safe and effective hair loss treatment, you could open up a significant market."
However, whether this becomes the "next GLP-1" remains uncertain. Drug development carries a high risk of clinical failure, and unlike obesity, hair loss has relatively lower medical necessity, making insurance coverage difficult to obtain. This means consumers would likely bear the full cost. Historically, numerous obesity treatments have emerged, but many failed to become blockbuster drugs, and some companies even went bankrupt.
Despite these risks, analysts remain optimistic about further upside. Needham's Blum said of Absci, "This is an all-or-nothing story. It's still cheap, so I'd buy it now."

Aurobindo Pharma Sets Up Auropharm Overseas to Expand Pharma Manufacturing, Marketing
Written By :
Parthika Patel
Published On
2026-08-29T23:50:50+05:30
|
Updated On
29 Aug 2026 11:50 PM IST
Hyderabad
: Aurobindo Pharma Limited has incorporated a new wholly owned subsidiary, Auropharm Overseas Limited, in India, with the objective of undertaking manufacturing and marketing operations in India and foreign countries.
Auropharm Overseas Limited was incorporated on August 13, 2026, and therefore has no applicable turnover history. The new entity belongs to the pharmaceuticals industry and has been established as a wholly owned subsidiary of Aurobindo Pharma.
According to the company's disclosure, the incorporation of Auropharm Overseas Limited is considered a related party transaction, as the entity is a wholly owned subsidiary of Aurobindo Pharma. However, the company's promoters and promoter group do not have any interest in the transaction.
The primary objective behind establishing the subsidiary is to undertake manufacturing and marketing operations in India as well as foreign countries. The company has not indicated any business activity outside the pharmaceutical sector for the newly incorporated entity.
Also Read: Merck Signs Voluntary Licensing Deals with 7 Generic Drugmakers for Affordable HIV Pill in 129 Countries
Aurobindo Pharma stated that no governmental or regulatory approvals are required for the incorporation. The indicative time period for completion of the acquisition has been marked as not applicable, as the transaction relates to the incorporation of a new wholly owned subsidiary rather than an acquisition of an existing entity.
The nature of consideration for the incorporation is 100% subscription to the share capital in cash. The initial subscription to the share capital is ₹10,00,000, divided into 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. Aurobindo Pharma holds 100% shareholding and control in the newly incorporated company.
Auropharm Overseas Limited is a newly incorporated company, and consequently its history of turnover for the previous three years is not available. The disclosure specifically confirms that the company was incorporated in India on August 13, 2026.
The incorporation of Auropharm Overseas Limited establishes a new wholly owned pharmaceutical subsidiary of Aurobindo Pharma, with its stated business objective focused on manufacturing and marketing operations in India and foreign countries. The subsidiary has been funded through an initial cash subscription of ₹10 lakh for 1 lakh equity shares, with Aurobindo Pharma holding 100% control.

 ACG co-founder Jasjit Singh dies at 83 after six decades of contribution to pharma manufacturing
 Our Bureau, Mumbai
 Saturday, August 29, 2026, 14:30 Hrs  [IST]
 ACG co-founder and vice chairman Jasjit Singh, who played a central role in building the company from a small capsule manufacturing operation in Mumbai into a global pharmaceutical manufacturing solutions group, passed away on August 27, 2026, at the age of 83.
The pharmaceutical industry has mourned the passing of Singh, remembering him as an engineer, entrepreneur, industrialist and pioneer who contributed to the development of India’s pharmaceutical manufacturing ecosystem over more than six decades.
Singh founded ACG in 1961 along with his elder brother, Ajit Singh. The company began with a small capsule manufacturing operation in Kandivali, Mumbai, and subsequently expanded its presence to serve pharmaceutical and nutraceutical manufacturers in markets across the world. His association with the company spanned more than six decades, during which he remained closely involved in its growth, technological development and culture of innovation.
For ACG, Singh’s passing marks the loss of one of the individuals who was present at the beginning of the company’s journey and remained associated with its evolution over more than 60 years. For the pharmaceutical industry, his life represents the contribution of an entrepreneur who helped develop manufacturing capabilities and supported the transition of Indian pharmaceutical ancillary manufacturing from a small domestic activity to a globally connected industry.

Pharma Associations.content:
KSDMSMA adopts pooled procurement, last-mile delivery, backs Made-in-Nigeria drugs
By Rotimi Odofin
Kogi State is quietly rewriting the story of medicine access, affordability and supply security, with the state government adopting a coordinated procurement system designed to make quality drugs available, affordable and accessible to residents across the three senatorial districts.
At the centre of the emerging transformation is the Kogi State Drugs and Medical Supplies Management Agency (KSDMSMA), which, under the administration of Governor Alhaji Ahmed Usman Ododo, has moved away from fragmented drug purchasing towards a more unified and strategic supply-chain model.
The objective is straightforward but far-reaching: quality medicines at the right price, in the right quantity and at the right time—irrespective of where a patient seeks treatment in Kogi State.
The breakthrough is being driven through the Group Purchasing Framework (GPF), a coordinated procurement initiative involving 19 member Drugs Management Organisations across Nigeria and 30 pre-qualified suppliers supporting procurement across 81 essential healthcare commodity categories.
The framework was developed through collaboration among the Nigeria Health Commissioners’ Forum (NHCF), Forum of Drugs Management Agencies (DMAs), and Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Group of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (PMG-MAN), with facilitation by the African Resource Centre for Excellence in Supply Chain Management (ARC-ESM).
According to the GPF Mid-Year Implementation Report by ARC-ESM, ₦132.3 billion was deployed under the first coordinated annual pooled procurement exercise, creating a stronger collective purchasing position and providing the volume needed for improved price negotiations with pharmaceutical manufacturers.
For Kogi, the implications are significant.
Bulk purchasing and direct engagement with manufacturers are helping to secure better prices, improved quality assurance, agreed payment terms, faster delivery and more dependable supply, thereby reducing the perennial problem of medicine stock-outs.
The Executive Secretary of KSDMSMA, Pharm. Ibrahim Onize Salamat, with the backing of the Coordinating Commissioner for Health, Dr. Abdulazeez Adams Adeiza, has positioned the GPF as a major instrument for strengthening medicine security and building a more resilient health supply chain for the state.
Rather than allowing individual health facilities to operate largely as separate purchasing points, the new approach seeks to establish a more coordinated system capable of leveraging the purchasing power of the entire state.
FROM WAREHOUSE TO HOSPITALS
The reform is not stopping at procurement.
Through the Last Mile Delivery (LMD) approach, third-quarter supplies have already been delivered directly to hospitals and health institutions across Kogi Central, Kogi East and Kogi West.
The strategy is designed to eliminate unnecessary delays between procurement, distribution and the point where medicines are ultimately required—health facilities and patients.
A supply mop-up exercise is also ongoing to strengthen stock levels and ensure that facilities have adequate medicines to respond to patient needs.
The emerging system is therefore addressing two sides of the medicine-access challenge simultaneously: the cost of medicines and the reliability of their availability.
MADE-IN-NIGERIA GETS A BOOST
Beyond affordability and availability, Kogi’s medicine strategy is also aligning with the Federal Government’s drive to strengthen domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing.
The state is deliberately opening its procurement space to more Nigerian pharmaceutical companies, creating opportunities for local manufacturers while strengthening the country’s broader medicine-security architecture.
As of August 26, 2026, an additional 10 Nigerian pharmaceutical companies had been registered by the Bureau of Public Procurement in the state and pre-qualified by KSDMSMA to supply quality-assured medicines to public health facilities.
More pharmaceutical manufacturers are reportedly processing their membership and qualification requirements.
For Kogi, the policy carries a double advantage: expanding the pool of reliable medicine suppliers while supporting the growth of Nigeria’s domestic pharmaceutical industry.
FROM NATIONAL FORUMS TO KOGI’S HEALTH FACILITIES
KSDMSMA’s strategy has also been informed by active participation in national conversations around medicine security and supply-chain reform.
In 2026, the agency was represented at major national engagements, including the 6th Annual Leadership Breakfast Meeting in Abuja on Universal Medicine Security and the Nigeria Supply Chain Summit in Lagos, where stakeholders examined the future of medicine access and supply-chain management.
The engagements provide opportunities for Kogi to exchange knowledge, learn from emerging best practices and adapt successful approaches to the state’s own healthcare realities.
ONE PRICE, ONE SYSTEM, ONE KOGI
Perhaps the most ambitious aspect of the reform is the push for a single, centralised medicine supply-chain system across the state.
KSDMSMA is intensifying advocacy for full compliance by Heads of Health Institutions, in line with the broader policy direction of the Nigeria Governors’ Forum.
The ultimate target is a uniform pricing regime under which the same medicine would not be sold at significantly different prices simply because a patient moved from one public health facility to another.
From primary healthcare centres to secondary and tertiary institutions, the agency wants Kogi residents to benefit from a more transparent and predictable medicine pricing structure.
That ambition, if fully implemented, could represent one of the most consequential reforms in Kogi’s public health supply chain.
THE ROAD AHEAD
For KSDMSMA, the reform is not being presented as a destination but as the foundation for a stronger medicine-security system.
The agency’s focus remains clear: quality drugs must be available, affordable and accessible to every Kogi resident.
The combination of pooled procurement, stronger manufacturer relationships, last-mile delivery, tighter quality control, local pharmaceutical participation and centralised supply-chain management is creating what officials describe as a more efficient and resilient medicine ecosystem.
The agency has expressed appreciation to Governor Ahmed Usman Ododo for his commitment to strengthening the state’s health supply chain, as well as to the Coordinating Commissioner for Health, Dr. Abdulazeez Adams Adeiza, Heads of Health Institutions, KSDMSMA staff and the agency’s strategic partners.
Partners including PMG-MAN, ARC-ESM, NHCF, other Drugs Management Agencies and pharmaceutical distributors have all played roles in the evolving system.
If the momentum is sustained, the significance of the 2026 reforms could extend beyond simply putting more medicines on hospital shelves.
It could mean building a system in which a patient in Kogi East, Kogi Central or Kogi West has a better chance of finding the medicine they need, at a fairer price, with stronger assurance of quality—and without being forced to bear the burden of a fragmented supply chain.
For Kogi State, the message is increasingly clear:
Medicine security is no longer being treated as an afterthought. It is becoming a central pillar of the state’s healthcare reform agenda.

Pharma Associations.content:
Teva Pharmaceutical Industries (NYSE:TEVA) agreed to acquire a neuroscience asset from BioXcel Therapeutics involving a sublingual film for agitation in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder patients through a court supervised bankruptcy sale.
The product is under FDA review, and the transaction remains subject to court approval as of late August 2026.
The deal aligns with Teva's stated Pivot to Growth strategy and adds to its focus on neuroscience treatments.

Teva Pharmaceutical Industries develops and distributes generic medicines and biopharmaceutical products across the US, Europe, Israel, and other international markets. This neuroscience deal therefore fits within a broad drug portfolio rather than a narrow focus on one therapy area or geography.
3 things going right for Teva Pharmaceutical Industries that this headline doesn't cover.

How does this BioXcel neuroscience asset fit into Teva Pharmaceutical Industries' recent moves?
The BioXcel sublingual film slots alongside Teva Pharmaceutical Industries' broader neuroscience push, which already includes ecopipam for pediatric Tourette syndrome under FDA review with a Priority Review and Orphan Drug designation. Together these assets deepen Teva's presence in central nervous system disorders and extend its Pivot to Growth focus on specialty, higher margin therapies.
Does this transaction change the existing Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Narrative in a meaningful way?
This news mainly reinforces the existing Narrative rather than overturning it. The BioXcel deal adds another branded neuroscience asset that supports the catalyst around expanding higher margin products and business development, while the key Narrative risks such as heavy debt and reliance on a smaller group of branded drugs still require close attention.
If we take a look at the
community Narrative for Teva Pharmaceutical Industries
, we can see how this news fits into the bigger investment story.
What should investors watch next for this BioXcel deal to really matter for Teva?
The immediate focus is on two milestones. One is bankruptcy court approval and closing of the BioXcel asset purchase on the agreed terms of up to US$125m. The other is the FDA review outcome for the sublingual film, which will determine whether Teva can actually bring this product to patients.

GDPR was designed to constrain large platforms and increased their share of the European ad market, because compliance cost fell hardest on small intermediaries. The FTC's antitrust case, the one that could genuinely have broken the company up, was decided in Meta's favour last November. The only thing that ever meaningfully hurt the business was Apple changing a tracking default, and Meta out-spent that too, while the ad-tech firms that could not afford to rebuild disappeared. Flexible Film Transfer Bags for Powders Market to Nearly Double by 2035 on Biologic Manufacturing Expansion
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global
Flexible Film Transfer Bags for Powders market
, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global market for flexible film transfer bags for powders is entering a sustained expansion phase, with demand projected to grow at a compound annual rate of 7-9% from 2026 to 2035, roughly doubling in volume by the end of the forecast period. This growth is anchored in the accelerating adoption of single-use technology (SUT) across clinical and commercial drug manufacturing, which transforms what was once a capital equipment purchase into a recurring consumables stream.
High-purity and specialty film grades, serving sterile pharmaceutical and advanced therapy applications, now account for an estimated 70% of market value and are expected to capture over 80% by 2035, driven by regulatory tightening and increasing drug product complexity. Supply remains structurally concentrated in cleanroom fabrication facilities in North America and Europe, creating import dependence for rapidly growing Asia-Pacific markets, which incur logistics cost penalties of 5-12% of product value to secure validated transfer bag inventory.
Multi-layer co-extruded film architectures are displacing monolayer constructions, offering superior barrier properties, lower extractables profiles, and enhanced mechanical robustness for handling dense, abrasive, or high-potency powders. Buyers are expanding dual-source or multi-source qualification programs to mitigate supply risk, yet the 12- to 24-month validation cycle for alternative suppliers limits rapid diversification and reinforces the position of established vendors.
This report provides a comprehensive analysis of market size, growth trajectory, demand structure, supply capability, trade flows, pricing, competitive landscape, and forecast to 2035, offering a data-driven view for manufacturers, distributors, importers, exporters, investors, and strategy teams.
The baseline scenario for the flexible film transfer bags for powders market points to robust growth through 2035, underpinned by structural shifts in pharmaceutical and specialty chemical manufacturing. The market is projected to expand at a CAGR of 7-9% from 2026 to 2035, with volume nearly doubling from 2025 levels. High-purity and specialty film grades will drive value growth, capturing over 80% of market value by 2035, as regulatory standards tighten and drug product complexity increases. Single-use technology adoption is the primary catalyst, converting rigid container systems into recurring consumables demand.
Multi-layer co-extruded films are becoming the standard, offering improved barrier properties and lower extractables, which is critical for high-potency and aseptic applications. Supply remains concentrated in North America and Europe, with cleanroom fabrication facilities operating at 80-90% utilisation, leading to extended lead times of 20-30 weeks for fully documented sterile assemblies. This creates import dependence for Asia-Pacific markets, which face logistics cost penalties of 5-12% of product value. Feedstock resin price volatility, with cumulative increases of 15-20% over 2021-2025, compresses margins for non-differentiated suppliers. Regulatory divergence across USP, Ph.
Eur., and JP, along with evolving GMP Annex 1 requirements, imposes significant documentation burdens. Despite these challenges, the market is set for sustained growth, driven by biologic drug manufacturing expansion, advanced therapy development, and the ongoing shift toward single-use systems.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
Accelerating adoption of single-use technology (SUT) in pharmaceutical manufacturing, converting capital equipment purchases into recurring consumables demand.
Global expansion of biologic drug manufacturing and aseptic powder processing capacity, driving demand for high-purity transfer bags.
Regulatory tightening and evolving GMP Annex 1 requirements, increasing the need for validated, documented single-use systems.
Multi-layer co-extruded film architectures offering superior barrier properties and lower extractables, replacing monolayer constructions.
Growing complexity of drug products, including high-potency and advanced therapy formulations, requiring specialty film grades.
Rising demand for flexible packaging in food ingredient and specialty chemical sectors, supporting volume growth.
Potential Growth Constraints
Cleanroom fabrication capacity operating at 80-90% utilisation, leading to extended lead times of 20-30 weeks for sterile assemblies.
Volatile feedstock resin prices for virgin medical-grade polypropylene and polyethylene, compressing margins for non-differentiated suppliers.
Divergent regulatory expectations across major pharmacopoeias (USP, Ph. Eur., JP) and evolving GMP Annex 1 requirements, raising compliance costs.
12- to 24-month validation cycles for alternative suppliers limit rapid diversification and reinforce incumbent positions.
Logistics cost penalties of 5-12% of product value for Asia-Pacific markets due to import dependence on North American and European suppliers.
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
Pharmaceutical Manufacturing (estimated share: 55%)
Pharmaceutical manufacturing is the largest end-use sector for flexible film transfer bags for powders, accounting for 55% of market value. The segment is driven by the global expansion of biologic drug manufacturing and aseptic powder processing capacity. Single-use technology adoption is accelerating across clinical and commercial manufacturing, converting rigid container systems into recurring consumables demand. High-purity and specialty film grades are essential for sterile and high-potency applications, with regulatory tightening and drug product complexity pushing demand toward multi-layer co-extruded films.
Through 2035, the sector is expected to maintain its dominance, with value share potentially exceeding 60% as advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs) and personalized medicines gain traction. Demand-side indicators include the number of FDA and EMA approvals for biologics, capacity expansion announcements by CDMOs, and the pace of SUT adoption in new facilities. Current trend: Dominant and growing, driven by biologic drug manufacturing and single-use technology adoption..
Major trends:
Single-use technology adoption in clinical and commercial manufacturing, Shift toward multi-layer co-extruded films for enhanced barrier and extractables performance, Increasing use of high-purity and specialty grades for high-potency and aseptic applications, and Expansion of biologic drug manufacturing capacity globally.
Representative participants:
Thermo Fisher Scientific, Sartorius AG, Merck KGaA, Entegris, and Saint-Gobain.
Biopharmaceutical & Advanced Therapy (estimated share: 20%)
Biopharmaceutical and advanced therapy manufacturing is the fastest-growing end-use segment, representing 20% of market value. This segment includes the production of cell and gene therapies, monoclonal antibodies, and other advanced biologics that require highly controlled, aseptic powder handling. The demand for flexible film transfer bags here is driven by the need for single-use, sterile, and validated containment solutions that minimize contamination risk and cross-contamination. As advanced therapies move from clinical to commercial scale, the demand for high-purity and specialty film grades is surging.
The segment is expected to grow at a double-digit rate through 2035, supported by increasing regulatory approvals and the expansion of manufacturing capacity for ATMPs. Key demand-side indicators include the number of clinical trials, commercial launches, and capacity investments by CDMOs and biotech firms. Current trend: Fastest-growing segment, driven by advanced therapy medicinal products and cell/gene therapies..
Major trends:
Rapid growth of cell and gene therapies requiring sterile powder transfer, Increasing adoption of single-use systems in ATMP manufacturing, Demand for high-purity films with low extractables and leachables, and Expansion of commercial-scale manufacturing capacity for advanced therapies.
Representative participants:
Thermo Fisher Scientific, Sartorius AG, Merck KGaA, Corning Incorporated, and Entegris.
Food & Beverage Ingredients (estimated share: 12%)
The food and beverage ingredients sector accounts for 12% of market value, using flexible film transfer bags for handling powdered ingredients such as flavors, additives, and nutritional supplements. The segment is driven by the need for hygienic, efficient, and cost-effective powder transfer solutions that reduce contamination risk and improve operational efficiency. While not as stringent as pharmaceutical applications, food-grade transfer bags must meet food safety regulations and often require barrier properties to protect against moisture and oxygen. The segment is expected to grow steadily, supported by the expansion of processed food and beverage production, particularly in emerging markets.
Demand-side indicators include food production volumes, investment in automated processing lines, and regulatory standards for food contact materials. Current trend: Stable growth, driven by demand for hygienic and efficient powder handling in food processing..
Major trends:

The specialty chemicals sector represents 8% of market value, using flexible film transfer bags for handling a wide range of powdered chemicals, including pigments, catalysts, and additives. The segment is driven by the need for safe, contained, and efficient transfer of powders that may be reactive, hazardous, or sensitive to moisture. Flexible film bags offer advantages over rigid containers in terms of disposability, reduced cleaning requirements, and lower risk of cross-contamination. The segment is expected to grow moderately, supported by the expansion of specialty chemical production, particularly in Asia-Pacific.
Demand-side indicators include chemical production indices, investment in new production capacity, and regulatory requirements for safe handling of hazardous materials. Current trend: Moderate growth, driven by demand for safe handling of reactive or hazardous powders..

Increasing focus on worker safety and containment in chemical handling, Adoption of single-use systems to reduce cleaning and cross-contamination risks, Growth in specialty chemical production in emerging markets, and Development of films with enhanced chemical resistance and barrier properties.

Nutraceuticals & Cosmetics (estimated share: 5%)

The segment is expected to grow steadily, supported by the expansion of the nutraceutical and cosmetics industries, particularly in North America and Europe.

Regional Dynamics
Asia-Pacific (estimated share: 35%)
Asia-Pacific is the largest and fastest-growing market, driven by rapid expansion of biopharmaceutical manufacturing, particularly in China, India, and South Korea. The region faces import dependence on North American and European suppliers, incurring logistics cost penalties of 5-12% of product value. Local cleanroom capacity is developing but remains insufficient to meet demand, creating opportunities for international suppliers. Growth is supported by government initiatives to boost domestic pharmaceutical production and increasing adoption of single-use technology. Direction: Fastest-growing region, driven by biopharmaceutical manufacturing expansion and increasing SUT adoption..
North America (estimated share: 30%)
North America holds a significant share, with the United States being a major producer and consumer. The region benefits from a strong biopharmaceutical sector, with high adoption of single-use technology and stringent regulatory standards. Cleanroom fabrication capacity is concentrated here, supporting domestic supply. Growth is driven by the expansion of biologic manufacturing and advanced therapies, though market saturation and competition from lower-cost regions pose challenges. Direction: Mature but steady growth, driven by advanced therapy development and regulatory standards..
Europe (estimated share: 25%)
Europe is a key market, with strong demand from pharmaceutical and specialty chemical sectors. The region is home to major cleanroom fabrication facilities and benefits from a well-established regulatory framework. Growth is driven by the expansion of biologics manufacturing and the adoption of single-use technology. However, regulatory divergence across EU member states and Brexit-related changes create compliance complexities. The market is expected to grow steadily, with a focus on high-purity and specialty grades. Direction: Stable growth, supported by pharmaceutical innovation and regulatory harmonization..
Latin America (estimated share: 6%)
Latin America is a smaller but growing market, with demand driven by the expansion of pharmaceutical and food processing industries in Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina. The region relies heavily on imports, particularly from North America and Europe, due to limited local cleanroom capacity. Growth is supported by increasing healthcare investment and the adoption of single-use technology, though economic volatility and infrastructure challenges remain. Direction: Emerging market with moderate growth, driven by pharmaceutical and food processing expansion..
Middle East & Africa (estimated share: 4%)
The Middle East and Africa region is at an early stage of adoption, with demand primarily from pharmaceutical and food processing sectors. Growth is driven by healthcare infrastructure development, particularly in Gulf Cooperation Council countries, and increasing investment in local manufacturing. The market is small but offers opportunities for suppliers willing to navigate regulatory and logistical challenges. Import dependence is high, and lead times are longer, but the region is expected to grow steadily through 2035. Direction: Nascent market with gradual growth, driven by healthcare infrastructure development..

Teva (TEVA) Stock Looks Below Fair Value While Earnings Sit Above Fair Value
Bailey Pemberton
Sun, 30 August 2026 at 11:14 am GMT+9
6 min read
TEVA
BTAI
TEVA
Teva Pharmaceutical Industries stock has delivered a very strong 284.4% gain over the past 5 years, yet current checks send mixed signals as the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) estimate points to undervaluation while market based multiples screen the shares as expensive. Investors looking at Teva today see a stock with powerful recent momentum against a low overall value score that suggests it is not a straightforward bargain.
A 284.4% return over 5 years highlights how much Teva has already rewarded long term holders, which can make fresh entry points more sensitive to valuation.
Recent moves to expand the neuroscience portfolio, including the agreed acquisition of BioXcel Therapeutics' dexmedetomidine sublingual film and the FDA priority review for ecopipam in pediatric Tourette syndrome, can support expectations for future cash flows, while ongoing patent litigation outcomes and generic competition risk may still weigh on how durable those cash flows are seen to be.
Teva scores
2 out of 6
on a broad value screen, which leans expensive overall even though the intrinsic value estimate suggests the share price trades at a 43.7% discount.
The issue now is whether Teva Pharmaceutical Industries' current price already reflects the recent progress and pipeline news, or if the gap to the intrinsic value estimate leaves room for further upside.
Spot opportunities beyond Teva Pharmaceutical Industries by scanning our hand picked list of
44 high quality undervalued stocks
that also combine strong recent momentum with discounted cash flow support.
Does Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Look Undervalued on Cash Flow?
The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model values Teva Pharmaceutical Industries by projecting future free cash flows and discounting them back to today. Teva currently reports latest twelve month free cash flow of about $1.37b, and the model assumes these cash flows continue to grow rather than contract over the coming decade.
On this basis, the DCF framework points to an estimated intrinsic value of about $64.78 per share in $ terms. That compares to the current share price, which implies the stock trades at roughly a 43.7% discount and appears undervalued on this metric. The FDA priority review for ecopipam helps explain why some investors may already be optimistic, yet the share price still sits well below what the cash flow projections support.
Overall, the DCF work suggests Teva Pharmaceutical Industries stock currently appears undervalued relative to its projected cash generation.

Has Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Run Too Far on Earnings?
P/E is often the go to check for Teva Pharmaceutical Industries because earnings are a key focus for established pharmaceutical businesses. On this measure, Teva trades on a P/E of about 60.1x, which is far above both the pharmaceuticals industry average of 16.7x and a peer group average of 19.3x.
The tailored fair P/E ratio for Teva is estimated at 34.1x, which already reflects its sector, risk profile and business mix. The current 60.1x multiple sits well above that level. As a result, the stock screens as expensive compared with what this framework would typically support for Teva.
On the P/E check, Teva Pharmaceutical Industries stock appears overvalued relative to both its fair multiple and its sector benchmarks.

The Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Narrative: What Would Justify Today's Price?
Simply Wall St Narratives for Teva Pharmaceutical Industries pick up where this valuation puzzle leaves off and explain what future growth, margins and earnings would need to look like for the stock to be worth materially more or materially less than today's price. Each Narrative links a fair value to a specific storyline about Teva Pharmaceutical Industries' potential catalysts and risks so you can track which scenario seems to be unfolding over time on the Community page.
Community narratives on Teva Pharmaceutical Industries sit far apart, with one side focused on a portfolio and margin story and the other on concentration and execution risk.
Bull case: 11% undervalued
"Teva's strategic focus and rapid execution on expanding its innovative branded products (AUSTEDO, AJOVY, UZEDY, and upcoming olanzapine LAI), combined with a robust late-stage pipeline targeting large patient populations, are expected to drive higher-margin topline growth and a more profitable product mix, supporting gross margin and net earnings expansion."

to see why Teva Pharmaceutical Industries could be undervalued
Bear case: 10% overvalued
"Heavy reliance on a narrow set of growth engines such as AUSTEDO, UZEDY and AJOVY, in indications where underdiagnosis and undertreatment are being actively addressed across the industry, could expose Teva to future competitive launches and reimbursement tightening that may cap pricing power and slow top line expansion, pressuring revenue growth targets."
Read the full Bear Case
to see why Teva Pharmaceutical Industries could be overvalued

Head over to our Community to see what others are saying!
The Bottom Line
Teva Pharmaceutical Industries presents a split picture. The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) work points to meaningful intrinsic value upside, while the P/E based view screens the stock as overvalued compared with sector and tailored fair multiples. That mismatch reflects a cash flow story that looks stronger than what current earnings multiples imply. However, the broader low value score signals that most other checks are not supportive. The key question from here is whether Teva can deliver the cash flow, margin and pipeline execution needed to close that gap, or whether the current discount to intrinsic value is the market pricing in ongoing risk around competition and legal outcomes.
